questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Why A Generator Gives Up Control
questions.learningObjective: explain what suspending a generator buys over handing back a finished collection
questions.stem: A helper can produce a very long run of values from a source that is itself very long. Explain why suspending at each value is worth the extra machinery compared with building the whole run first and handing it back at the end.

answer.exemplar: The reason is that the two designs hold different amounts at once. Building the whole run first means every value exists before the caller has looked at any of them, so the memory needed is the size of the entire result, and a source that never ends is simply not usable. Suspending at each value means the only thing that exists at any moment is the position inside the helper plus the value being handed over, so the memory needed is a small constant no matter how long the run is, and a source that never ends becomes perfectly usable because nothing ever asks for all of it at once. The second thing suspending buys is control over when the next piece of work happens. A caller that stops after the first three values causes the helper to stop after producing three, so no further reading, parsing or transforming is done at all. With a finished list, the work of producing the tail has already been paid for whether the caller wants it or not, which is why the finished-list version keeps paying for rows nobody will read. There is a cost to suspending that is worth naming honestly. Keeping a position alive means the helper's names stay alive too, and anything the helper is holding stays alive as long as the walk is, so a helper that captured something large in a closure keeps that large thing pinned for the whole run. Saving that state also means a frame object per live walk, so a program that starts a very large number of walks at once pays for all of them. Suspending is also less obvious to read, because the body reads top to bottom but executes in pieces, and a mistake part way through can leave a walk in a state that is hard to reason about from the source alone. There is a third design worth mentioning, which is handing back an object that computes its values on demand without a saved frame per walk, and that is a good fit when the state is small and the code needs to read plainly. The choice in practice comes down to a simple question: does the result need to be revisited more than once, and does its size matter? A result that is walked twice, indexed, sorted or measured needs a real collection behind it, because a generator gives its values out once and is then spent. A result that is walked once from a large or unbounded source is the case suspending was built for, and converting it to a list there trades a constant memory cost for a cost that grows with the source.

questions.explanation: Suspending means the memory needed is a small constant no matter how long the run is, and a caller that stops early stops the work rather than merely ignoring it, whereas a finished list is paid for in full before the first value is read. The cost is honest too: the helper's names and anything its closure captured stay alive for the life of the walk, and a walk can only be read once, so a result that must be revisited needs a real collection behind it.
questions.hint: Ask what exists in memory at each moment in the two designs, and what happens when the caller stops early.

questions.topic: What A Default Argument Is Bound To
questions.learningObjective: explain when a default argument is worked out and what that is good for and bad for
questions.stem: A parameter with a default can be written as a plain value, as a call to something, or as a collection written out. Explain when that default is worked out, what that buys, and what it costs.

answer.exemplar: The moment is the one that explains everything else: the default is worked out once, while the function is being defined, and the resulting object is reused by every call that does not supply the value. It is not worked out per call, and this is worth being precise about because the two designs behave differently in ways that matter. What it buys is that a default is genuinely free at call time, so a parameter that almost every caller overrides costs nothing for the callers who do override it. A default that calls a function is the clearest case, because the call happens at import time rather than on every invocation, which is a real saving when the value is expensive. What it costs is that a default holding a mutable object is shared by every call, so anything a call does to that object is visible to every later call, and the usual symptom is a value that keeps growing or a setting that cannot be turned off. The failure is quiet, which is the worst part of it: nothing complains, the result is merely wrong in a way that looks like a logic mistake somewhere else. The repair is to move the mutable value inside the body, so each call builds its own, and that costs one line and nothing else. There is a second cost that is less obvious, which is that a default is worked out at definition time whether or not any caller ever needs it, so a default that reads a setting or touches the environment is captured at import time and will not notice a later change. For a value that is meant to be configurable while the program runs, the right home is the body, not the signature. One thing defaults are genuinely good for is a sentinel that means not supplied, which is different from a default that means a real value. A caller who wants to pass the value that happens to be the default needs a way to say so, and a bare object used only for that comparison is the usual way to say it, which is a legitimate use that is easy to confuse with the mistake above. The distinction to hold on to is between a default that describes a value and a default that describes a state. Values are safe to share; state is not, because state changes and a shared copy of it changes for everyone.

questions.explanation: The default is worked out once at definition time, so the same object serves every call that does not supply a value, which makes an expensive default free at call time and a mutable default silently shared. Moving a mutable default into the body fixes the sharing at the cost of one line, and a default that must reflect a setting the program can change belongs in the body rather than in the signature.

questions.topic: What The Copying Helper Does Not Fix

questions.stem: A decorator returns a new function that calls the old one, and there is a helper in the standard library that copies the recorded details across. Explain what that copy does for a reader of the code and what it does not repair.

answer.exemplar: What the copy repairs is everything a tool reads without running the function. A name, a docstring, a recorded signature, the module the function came from and the annotations attached to it are all read off the object, and if the wrapper does not carry them then any of those readers sees the wrapper instead of the function, so every decorated function in a program reports under one name and none of them documents itself. Copying them across costs one line and removes a whole class of confusion, which is why the helper exists and why its use is close to automatic. What the copy does not repair is anything about how the call actually behaves, and this is where a wrapper's real cost lives. The wrapper is a different function with a different signature, and the copy makes the original's signature visible rather than true, so a tool that inspects the signature sees the promise the wrapper intends to keep and not the promise it actually enforces. The wrapper also has a different performance shape: every call goes through one more layer, adds one more frame to any traceback, and does whatever the decorator was written to do, which may be work the original never did. A decorator that catches everything, or that retries, or that returns a cached result, changes the meaning of the function, and no amount of copying details communicates that. A decorator that is not careful about its own signature will accept calls the original refused, because the wrapper's parameters are ordinary ones unless the wrapper was written to match, and this is the more common surprise. There is a third thing worth naming, which is what happens when the decorated function is used as something other than a call. A wrapper built on an ordinary closure captures the original, so the original stays alive as long as the wrapper does, which matters for a function that holds a large cache. A wrapper built on a class behaves differently again, and can be told apart by asking whether the decorated result is an instance. The practical advice is short: copy the details, keep the wrapper's signature as close to the original as the decorator's job allows, and make the decorator's own effect visible in its name so nobody has to infer it from reading the body.

questions.topic: Why An Irrefutable Case Must Come Last
questions.learningObjective: explain why a catch-all case cannot be written above the cases it would swallow
questions.stem: A match statement offers specific cases and one case that fits anything, and a rule says the case that fits anything has to be written last. Explain that rule, say what would happen if it were broken, and describe what to do when the fallback is wanted earlier.

answer.exemplar: Cases are tried from the top, and the first one that fits is the one that runs, so a case that fits anything placed above a specific case will take every value before the specific case is ever offered a chance. The rule is not a style preference; it follows directly from the order of trying. A statement written that way is also not a small waste, it is a hard error at the point the statement is compiled, and the message says the case is unreachable, which is a clearer failure than a program that quietly does the wrong thing. The reason the language insists rather than merely warning is that a catch-all placed early is always a mistake, never an intention, and a construct that can only mean a mistake is worth refusing outright. When the fallback really is wanted earlier, there are two honest routes. The first is to make the specific case fit only what it is meant to handle, by giving the case a guard, so that the value reaches the fallback because it genuinely does not match the earlier case rather than because the fallback was written too soon. That is the better route when the specific case has a condition that can be stated. The second is to use a plain conditional expression or a chain of tests instead of a match statement, which costs nothing and reads plainly when the branches are not really patterns at all. A third possibility, when several values should share a body, is to put them in one case using alternatives separated by the pattern separator, so the branch is expressed once and the ordering question does not arise. It is worth saying what the rule is not. It does not mean the last case must be a catch-all, because a statement whose cases all test something specific and that has no fallback is perfectly legal and simply does nothing for a value that fits none of them. And it does not mean a case can be skipped, because there is no way to jump past a case in the middle. The position rule and the ordering of the tests are the same fact seen from two sides, which is why the fix is always to reorder or to narrow, never to work around.

The honest fixes are to reorder, to narrow the specific case with a guard, to group several values into one case, or to use a plain test when the branches were never patterns.

answer.exemplar: What the helper gives up at a wait is the right to keep running. Everything the helper was doing stops at that line: its position is saved, its names stay alive, and the runner is free to do something else with the thread until the thing it was waiting for is ready. What the runner gains is the ability to hold several pieces of work at once on one thread, which is a real saving when the work is mostly spent waiting, because waiting on a network reply or a disk read releases the thread for another helper instead of blocking it. The cost is that the work is no longer a straight line of statements. The body of a helper is now a sequence of segments with yields between them, and a helper that does not await anywhere runs to completion in one go with no chance for anything else to interleave. That means an await is a statement about where interruption is allowed, and putting one in the wrong place changes behaviour rather than just speed. This is also why a blocking call in the same spot undoes the arrangement. A call that waits on the operating system, such as a sleep or a blocking read or a request made the ordinary way, does not hand control back to the runner, because it is not written as a wait the runner knows about. The thread is therefore pinned for exactly as long as the operation takes, every other helper on that runner is stuck behind it, and the concurrency the design was supposed to buy is simply absent. The symptom is easy to misread, because the program is correct and merely slow, with one helper's wait showing up as everybody's delay. A profile that shows one long blocking call and a runner that is otherwise idle is the signature. The repair is to make the blocking operation a wait the runner understands, and for most operations that means using the asynchronous form of the same library rather than a thread as a substitute. It is worth being clear that a thread is not a free replacement, because a thread that is blocked still costs a stack and still has to be scheduled, so a program that offloads every wait to threads trades the runner's problem for a much larger number of them. The clean arrangement is to await the operations that are genuinely waitable and to keep the genuinely blocking ones few and short.

questions.topic: Why A Signature Might Bar A Name
questions.learningObjective: explain the purpose a positional-only or name-only marker serves in a published signature
questions.stem: A published signature can forbid a caller from writing a parameter by name, or require it, and these markers were added to the language rather than left to convention. Explain what problem each one solves in a function other people call.

answer.exemplar: The problem both markers solve is freedom to change a function without breaking the people calling it, and it is worth separating the two because they buy that freedom in opposite directions. A parameter that must be given by position reserves the author's right to reorder it. If a caller may only write it as a value in a fixed slot, then inserting a new parameter before it, or reordering the existing ones, changes nothing an existing caller can detect, because the caller's values still land in the same slots. A parameter that may be given either way makes its position part of the published contract, so reordering it silently changes what a call means. The typical victims of that are two parameters of the same meaning that a reader can easily swap, and a parameter whose name collides with something the caller already has a use for. A name-only parameter buys the same freedom for a different resource. Once a parameter may only be named, the name itself becomes the only way to reach it, so the author can change its position, or add others beside it, without disturbing a caller, and a reader who writes it by name cannot accidentally hit it by position. The second benefit of a name-only parameter is that it documents an intent the position cannot carry, which is that the value is a setting rather than part of the main flow, and that it may be required or optional in a way a reader should not have to infer from the position alone. Neither marker is a restriction for its own sake, and both are worth using sparingly, because every marker a caller has to learn is a cost paid on every call. The pattern that works is to reserve the marker for the first few parameters of a function whose shape is well known and whose position carries meaning, and to leave the rest free. One thing these markers deliberately do not do is change the runtime cost of a call, and they are not a security boundary: a caller that genuinely wants to reach a barred parameter can reach it through the underlying object instead. They are an agreement between the author and the reader about how a function is meant to be called, and the language enforces the agreement because a convention this easy to break is a convention that will be broken.

questions.explanation: A position-only parameter reserves the author's right to reorder the signature without silently changing what an existing call means, and a name-only parameter makes the name the only route to the value so the position can change and the intent is documented. Both buy freedom to evolve a published function, and both are enforced by the call machinery rather than left to convention, which is why they cost a caller something and should be used sparingly.
questions.hint: Ask what a caller can detect when a parameter moves, and which route to a value each marker leaves open.

questions.learningObjective: compute a packed number from a comprehension that binds a name inside its own condition
questions.stem:
A comprehension keeps the values that pass a test, and the test binds a name as it goes, and the printed number packs the count of kept values in the hundreds and their sum and the leftover name in the tens and units. What number is printed?

values = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
kept = [x * 2 for x in values if (y := x) > 3]
print(len(kept) * 100 + sum(kept) + y)
questions.explanation: The test binds the name for every value it examines, not only the ones that pass, so after the walk the name holds the last value the test looked at, which is the last of the six. The kept values are the ones above three, doubled, so there are three of them and they sum to thirty. Packing the count in the hundreds with the sum in the tens and the leftover name in the units gives the printed number. This was executed with the interpreter, and the tempting answer of three hundred and thirty-nine comes from assuming the name holds the last value that passed the test rather than the last value the test saw, which is the whole subtlety of binding inside a test.
questions.hint: Ask how many times the test runs, and whether every run writes the name or only the passing ones.

fns = [lambda: i for i in range(4)]

questions.topic: Matching Sequences And Mappings With Guards
questions.learningObjective: trace a match statement over a list, a mapping and a plain value, using guards and a fallback
questions.stem:
One helper matches a list, a mapping and a plain value, with a guard on the first sequence case and on the first mapping case, and five values are passed in. Which pair names what this program prints and why?

def describe(v):
    match v:
        case [x] if x > 0:
            return 'one positive'
        case [x, y]:
            return f'two {x},{y}'
        case {'kind': k, 'n': n} if n > 1:
            return f'many {k}'
        case {'kind': k}:
            return f'single {k}'
        case _:
            return 'other'

for v in ([5], [1, 2], {'kind': 'x', 'n': 3}, {'kind': 'y', 'n': 1}, 'z'):
    print(describe(v))

options.text: one positive, two 1,2, many x, single y, other, because a guard that fails lets the next case be tried
one positive, one positive, many x, single y, other, because a failing guard falls back to the case it was on
options.misconception: believes a failing guard still selects its own case rather than the next one

options.text: other, two 1,2, many x, single y, other, because a one-item list never matches a list case
options.misconception: believes a list pattern only matches a list of two or more items

options.text: one positive, two 1,2, many x, many y, other, because the guard is only checked on sequence cases
options.misconception: believes a guard is ignored when the case matches a mapping

questions.explanation: A case runs only when the value fits its pattern and, if it has one, the guard also holds, so a value that fits the pattern but fails the guard is passed on to the next case rather than being reported by the one it failed. The one-item list of a positive value meets the first case, the two-item list has no match for one item so it falls to the second, the mapping with the larger count meets the guarded mapping case, the mapping with the smaller one fails that guard and is caught by the unguarded mapping case below it, and the plain text fits no pattern at all so the fallback reports it. This was executed with the interpreter, and the answer reusing the failed case is the belief to rule out first, because a guard is part of what it takes to select a case rather than something checked afterwards.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a value that fits a case's pattern but fails that case's guard.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Two Tasks Interleaving Around A Wait
questions.learningObjective: trace the printed order of two concurrent tasks and the order the gathered results arrive in
questions.stem:
Two tasks are scheduled and each announces when it starts and when it finishes after a wait, and the results are then gathered and printed. Which pair names what this program prints and why?

import asyncio

async def work(name, delay):
    print('start', name)
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    print('end', name)
    return name

async def main():
    a = asyncio.create_task(work('a', 0.02))
    b = asyncio.create_task(work('b', 0.01))
    return await asyncio.gather(a, b)

print(asyncio.run(main()))

options.text: start a, start b, end b, end a, then the two names in the order given, because a wait lets the other task run
start a, end a, start b, end b, then the two names, because the first task runs to its end before the second
options.misconception: believes scheduling a task makes it run straight through without interleaving

options.text: start a, start b, end b, end a, then b before a, because the results arrive in the order they finished
options.misconception: believes gathered results come back in order of finishing rather than of asking

options.text: start a, start b, end a, end b, then the two names, because the longer wait always finishes first
options.misconception: believes a longer wait somehow completes ahead of a shorter one

questions.explanation: Both tasks are scheduled before either reaches its wait, so the two start lines print first, and then the shorter wait is ready first so that task prints its end line and the other follows. The last print reports the two names in the order they were passed to the gathering call rather than the order they finished, which is the distinction the item turns on and the reason a caller who needs completion order has to ask for it. This was executed with the interpreter, and the answer reporting the finishing order is the belief to rule out first, because the gather is given a list of tasks and returns a list aligned to that list.
questions.hint: Ask which order the results are aligned to, and which wait becomes ready first.

questions.explanation: The comprehension runs with a scope of its own except that a name bound by an assignment expression inside it is deliberately allowed out to the surrounding code, which is the one exception to that rule and the reason the syntax exists at all. A plain function has no such exception, so its own binding stays inside it and reading that name in the surrounding code is caught and reported. This was executed with the interpreter, and the answer letting a function's local reach the caller is the belief to rule out first, because no ordinary local ever does.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two bindings is allowed to leave the scope that made it, and how many times each test runs.
